q: Where should you fire the engine to raise the far side of your orbit the most?
options: At the closest point to Earth
explain: You move fastest at the closest point (perigee), so the same push adds the most energy there. This is called the Oberth effect.
hint: You move fastest there, so each push counts most.

q: Which rocket launched Chandrayaan-3?
explain: ISRO's LVM3 rocket launched Chandrayaan-3 from Sriharikota on 14 July 2023.
hint: India's heaviest rocket, also called GSLV Mk III.

q: About how far away is the Moon?
explain: On average the Moon is about 384,400 km away. Light takes about 1.3 seconds to cross that gap.
hint: Light takes just over one second to cover it.

q: How long did Chandrayaan-3 take from launch to lunar orbit?
explain: Launched on 14 July, it entered lunar orbit on 5 August 2023: 22 days. Raising the orbit step by step saves fuel. Apollo needed the giant Saturn V to get there in 3 days.
hint: Launched 14 July, captured by the Moon on 5 August.

q: Why must a spacecraft brake to go into orbit around the Moon?
options: It arrives too fast for the Moon's gravity to hold it
explain: Without braking you would swing past the Moon and fly away. Slowing down at the closest point lets the Moon's gravity capture you.
hint: Think about speed: too fast to stay.

q: How strong is gravity on the Moon compared with Earth?
explain: The Moon's surface gravity is 1.62 m/s², about one-sixth of Earth's 9.81 m/s².
hint: You could jump about six times higher there.

q: Where on the Moon did Vikram land?
explain: Vikram landed near the lunar south pole on 23 August 2023, the first landing ever in that region.
hint: No country had landed there before.

q: What name was given to Vikram's landing spot?
explain: It is called Shiv Shakti Point. Chandrayaan-2's impact site is Tiranga Point, and Chandrayaan-1's probe hit Jawahar Point.
hint: It is named after a pair of Hindu deities.

q: Why can't a Moon lander use a parachute?
explain: A parachute needs air to push against. The Moon has almost no atmosphere, so only rocket engines can slow you down.
hint: Parachutes need something to push against.

q: How often do Earth and Mars line up for a fuel-saving trip?
explain: Earth laps Mars about every 780 days (26 months). That's when launch windows open.
hint: A bit more than two years.

q: How long did Mangalyaan take to fly from Earth to Mars?
explain: It left Earth orbit on 1 December 2013 and reached Mars on 24 September 2014, almost 300 days later.
hint: Launched November 2013, arrived September 2014.

q: Which country was the first to reach Mars orbit on its first try?
explain: India's Mangalyaan reached Mars orbit on 24 September 2014, on the country's first attempt.
hint: It is ISRO's own Mars mission.

q: Mangalyaan was famous for being…
explain: The mission cost about ₹450 crore (roughly US$74 million), famously less than the budget of the film Gravity.
hint: It cost less than many space films.

q: Why is a Mars landing called 'seven minutes of terror'?
options: Radio signals take minutes to reach Earth, so it must land all by itself
explain: Entry, parachute and landing take about 7 minutes, but radio needs several minutes to reach Earth. By the time we hear it started, it's already over.
hint: Mars is so far that a radio message takes minutes each way.

q: What lowered Perseverance gently onto Mars?
explain: A rocket-powered sky crane hovered and lowered the rover on 6.4 m cables, then flew away.
hint: It hung the rover on cables from a rocket-powered stage.

q: How thick is Mars' air compared with Earth's?
explain: Surface pressure on Mars is about 0.6% to 1% of Earth's. Parachutes help, but they can't land you alone.
hint: Very, very thin: barely any air.

q: How does a gravity assist speed up a spacecraft?
options: It borrows a tiny bit of the planet's orbital motion
Its engines fire near the planet
explain: Passing behind a moving planet, the craft gets pulled along and gains speed. The planet slows by an immeasurably tiny amount.
hint: The planet is moving round the Sun, and the spacecraft rides along a little.

q: Which is the only spacecraft to have visited Uranus and Neptune?
explain: Voyager 2 flew past Uranus in 1986 and Neptune in 1989, after Jupiter and Saturn.
hint: It flew past all four giant planets.

q: In which year was Voyager 2 launched?
explain: Voyager 2 launched on 20 August 1977. It is still sending data from interstellar space.
hint: The same year as Voyager 1.

q: What did Vikram do on 3 September 2023, after landing?
options: It hopped about 40 cm and landed again
explain: Vikram fired its engines, rose about 40 cm and landed 30–40 cm away, showing it could lift off again from the Moon.
hint: Lift off a little, land again a short way off.

q: Why was the hop important for future missions?
options: Missions that bring Moon samples back must lift off from the Moon
explain: Future sample-return and crewed missions must take off from the Moon. The hop proved the engines could restart there.
hint: Future sample-return missions must leave the Moon again.

q: What went wrong on Apollo 13?
explain: An oxygen tank exploded on the way to the Moon. The landing was cancelled and the crew flew around the Moon and home.
hint: It happened on the way to the Moon, 'Houston, we've had a problem'.

q: What happens if a capsule enters the air too shallowly?
options: It can skip off the atmosphere back into space
explain: Too shallow and it bounces off the top of the atmosphere, like a stone skipping on water. Too steep and it overheats.
hint: Think of a stone skipping on water.

q: Which spacecraft did the Apollo 13 crew use as a lifeboat?
explain: The crew moved into the Lunar Module Aquarius and used its engine and supplies to get home.
hint: The crew moved into the craft meant for the landing.

q: How fast must something go to escape Earth's gravity from its surface?
explain: Escape speed at Earth's surface is about 11.2 km/s, roughly 40,000 km/h. Higher up it is a little less.
hint: More than 40,000 km/h.

q: Why did Mangalyaan circle Earth for almost a month before leaving?
options: Its rocket was small, so it raised its orbit step by step
explain: The PSLV rocket put it in an Earth orbit. Mangalyaan then fired its engine at perigee several times to build up speed before escaping.
hint: Its rocket could not send it straight to Mars.

q: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
explain: Mercury orbits closest to the Sun, at about 58 million km.
hint: It is also the smallest planet.

q: Which is the largest planet?
explain: Jupiter is so big that more than 1,300 Earths could fit inside it.
hint: It is a gas giant, more than 11 times wider than Earth.

q: What is the Sun?
explain: The Sun is a star: a giant ball of hot gas powered by nuclear fusion.
hint: It is the closest one of its kind to us.

q: About how long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
explain: Light takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to travel the 150 million km from the Sun.
hint: Light travels about 150 million km to get here.

q: Who was the first human in space?
explain: Yuri Gagarin orbited Earth on 12 April 1961.
hint: He flew Vostok 1 in 1961.

q: Who was the first Indian in space?
explain: Rakesh Sharma flew on a Soviet Soyuz in April 1984.
hint: He flew on a Soviet spacecraft in 1984.

q: Which planet is known as the Red Planet?
explain: Iron oxide (rust) in its dust makes Mars look red.
hint: Rust (iron oxide) in its soil gives it its colour.

q: How many planets are in our Solar System?
explain: There are eight planets. Pluto has been classed as a dwarf planet since 2006.
hint: Pluto is no longer counted.

q: What was India's first satellite?
explain: Aryabhata was launched on 19 April 1975 by a Soviet rocket.
hint: Named after an ancient Indian astronomer and mathematician.

q: Where is India's main rocket launch centre?
explain: The Satish Dhawan Space Centre is at Sriharikota in Andhra Pradesh.
hint: It is on an island off the coast of Andhra Pradesh.

q: Which is the hottest planet?
explain: Venus's thick carbon-dioxide air traps heat, making it hotter than Mercury.
hint: It is not the closest to the Sun: its thick clouds trap heat.

q: What does a light-year measure?
explain: A light-year is the distance light travels in one year: about 9.5 trillion km.
hint: It is the distance light travels in one year.

q: What keeps the Moon in orbit around Earth?
explain: Earth's gravity keeps pulling the Moon, so it keeps falling around us instead of flying off.
hint: The same force that makes an apple fall.

q: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
explain: Neil Armstrong stepped onto the Moon on 20 July 1969 (21 July in UTC).
hint: He was the commander of Apollo 11.

q: Which is the largest moon in the Solar System?
explain: Jupiter's moon Ganymede is even bigger than the planet Mercury.
hint: It orbits Jupiter and is bigger than Mercury.

q: What does Aditya-L1 study?
explain: Aditya-L1 watches the Sun from the L1 point, 1.5 million km from Earth.
hint: 'Aditya' is a name for it in Sanskrit.

q: About how fast must you go to stay in orbit just above Earth?
explain: About 7.8 km/s, roughly 28,000 km/h. Fast enough that you keep falling around the curve of Earth.
hint: Much faster than any aeroplane: almost 8 km every second.

q: Why do we always see the same side of the Moon?
options: It spins once for every orbit
explain: The Moon is tidally locked: it turns once on its axis each time it orbits Earth.
hint: Its day and its orbit take the same time.

q: Which planet has the biggest, brightest rings?
explain: Saturn's rings are made of ice and rock, from tiny grains to house-sized chunks.
hint: The rings are made of ice and rock.

q: What do astronauts feel in orbit?
explain: Gravity is still about 90% as strong in low orbit. Astronauts float because they and their spacecraft are falling together.
hint: They are falling all the time, but moving sideways fast enough to miss the ground.

q: Which mission took the famous 'Earthrise' photo?
explain: Apollo 8, the first crewed flight around the Moon, in December 1968.
hint: The first crew to orbit the Moon, at Christmas 1968.

q: What was the Apollo 11 lunar module called?
explain: The lunar module was Eagle; the command module that stayed in orbit was Columbia.
hint: A bird that is a symbol of the USA.

q: Which rocket gave India its first satellite launch from Indian soil?
explain: SLV-3 put Rohini into orbit on 18 July 1980.
hint: India's first home-made satellite launcher.

q: What did Cassini drop onto Saturn's moon Titan?
explain: The European Huygens probe landed on Titan in January 2005: the farthest landing ever made.
hint: Named after a Dutch astronomer who studied Saturn.

q: What is the Moon Impact Probe's crash site called?
explain: Chandrayaan-1's probe hit near Shackleton crater on 14 November 2008, at Jawahar Point.
hint: Named after India's first Prime Minister.

q: What shape is the famous bright region on Pluto?
explain: The heart-shaped plain is called Tombaugh Regio, after Pluto's discoverer Clyde Tombaugh.
hint: Think of a symbol for love.

q: Juno is named after a goddess who could see through…
explain: In myth, Juno saw through the clouds Jupiter hid behind. The spacecraft also peers beneath Jupiter's clouds.
hint: In the myth she saw through the clouds Jupiter hid behind.

q: How many satellites did PSLV-C37 launch in one flight?
explain: 104 satellites on 15 February 2017, a world record at the time.
hint: A world record number of satellites at the time.

q: Why is docking in space tricky?
options: Nothing slows you down, so you must brake yourself
explain: With no air, a spacecraft keeps moving at the same speed until its thrusters change it. That's Newton's first law.
hint: Think about Newton's first law.

q: What is the far point of an orbit around Earth called?
explain: The far point is the apogee and the closest point is the perigee. Chandrayaan-3 raised its apogee step by step.
hint: Its partner word for the closest point is perigee.

q: What is the burn that sends a spacecraft from Earth orbit towards the Moon called?
explain: Trans-lunar injection (TLI) is the push that stretches the orbit all the way to the Moon. Chandrayaan-3 made it on 1 August 2023.
hint: Its short name is TLI.

q: About how long does the Moon take to go once around Earth?
explain: The Moon orbits Earth in about 27.3 days, which is why the month is roughly that long.
hint: Close to one month.

q: Which rocket launched Mangalyaan?
explain: ISRO’s PSLV-C25 launched Mangalyaan on 5 November 2013.
hint: ISRO’s workhorse rocket, which also launched Chandrayaan-1.

q: About how long did Mangalyaan’s braking burn at Mars last?
explain: On 24 September 2014 the engine fired for about 23 minutes, slowing Mangalyaan enough for Mars to catch it.
hint: Less than half an hour.

q: About how far sideways did Vikram land after its hop?
options: It landed in the same spot
explain: Vikram rose about 40 cm and landed about 30–40 cm away.
hint: About the length of a school ruler.

q: To leave Earth for Mars, which way did Mangalyaan fire its engine?
options: Forwards, the way it was moving
explain: Pushing in the direction you are moving (prograde) adds speed. Near Earth, where you move fastest, that extra speed counts most.
hint: To go faster, push the way you are already going.

q: Who took the Earthrise photo?
explain: Apollo 8 astronaut William Anders took the photo on 24 December 1968.
hint: His surname begins with A.

q: When was the Earthrise photo taken?
explain: Apollo 8 orbited the Moon over Christmas 1968, and the photo was taken on 24 December.
hint: The day before a big December holiday.

q: Who stayed in lunar orbit while Armstrong and Aldrin landed?
explain: Michael Collins flew the command module Columbia around the Moon while Eagle landed.
hint: His spacecraft was called Columbia.

q: In which year did Apollo 11 land on the Moon?
explain: Eagle landed on 20 July 1969.
hint: Exactly 50 years before Chandrayaan-2 was launched.

q: Who was the project director of SLV-3?
explain: Dr A.P.J. Abdul Kalam led the SLV-3 project, which put Rohini into orbit in 1980.
hint: He later became President of India.

q: About how heavy was the Rohini RS-1 satellite?
explain: Rohini RS-1 had a mass of about 35 kg.
hint: Lighter than most school students.

q: How long did Cassini study Saturn?
explain: Cassini orbited Saturn from 2004 until 2017.
hint: From 2004 until 2017.

q: How did Cassini’s mission end?
options: It dived into Saturn on purpose
explain: In 2017, low on fuel, Cassini was steered into Saturn so it could never crash onto a moon that might hold life.
hint: Planned so it could never hit a moon that might have life.

q: What did Chandrayaan-1 help discover on the Moon?
explain: Chandrayaan-1’s instruments, including NASA’s M3 on board, found signs of water molecules on the Moon.
hint: Something every living thing needs.

q: Which rocket launched Chandrayaan-1?
explain: PSLV-C11 launched Chandrayaan-1 on 22 October 2008.
hint: The same rocket family later launched Mangalyaan.

q: What is the heart-shaped region on Pluto named after?
explain: It is called Tombaugh Regio, after Clyde Tombaugh, who discovered Pluto in 1930.
hint: The astronomer who discovered Pluto.

q: Why is Pluto called a dwarf planet?
options: It has not cleared its path of other objects
It does not go round the Sun
explain: Pluto shares its region of space with many icy bodies, so since 2006 it is counted as a dwarf planet.
hint: It shares its region of space with many icy bodies.

q: What powers Juno so far from the Sun?
explain: Juno uses three large solar panels, the first solar-powered spacecraft to reach Jupiter.
hint: Sunlight, even though it is very dim out there.

q: Which giant storm on Jupiter does Juno study?
explain: The Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth that has raged for centuries.
hint: It is red and bigger than Earth.

q: What was the main satellite on PSLV-C37?
explain: Cartosat-2D, an Earth-observation satellite, flew with 103 smaller satellites.
hint: An Indian map-making satellite in the Cartosat series.

q: Why were the 104 satellites released in different directions?
options: Because the rocket was spinning by accident
So they would never bump into each other
explain: Each group was pushed off in a planned direction so the satellites drift apart safely.
hint: Safety first in a crowded orbit.

q: Which rocket launched SpaDeX?
explain: PSLV-C60 launched the two SpaDeX satellites on 30 December 2024.
hint: Flight number 60 of ISRO’s workhorse.

q: With SpaDeX, India became which country to dock in space?
explain: India docked in space after the USA, Russia and China.
hint: After the USA, Russia and China.

q: What did SRE-1 test?
options: Bringing a capsule back safely from orbit
explain: SRE-1 (Space capsule Recovery Experiment) was India’s first spacecraft to come back from orbit and be recovered.
hint: Its name has the word Recovery in it.

q: Where did SRE-1 splash down?
explain: It came down on parachutes in the Bay of Bengal, east of Sriharikota.
hint: The sea east of Chennai.

q: About how fast was SRE-1 moving when it hit the air?
explain: It entered the air at about 8 km/s, close to orbital speed, so it needed a heat shield.
hint: Close to orbital speed.

q: What is AstroSat?
explain: AstroSat is a telescope in orbit that looks at stars, galaxies and black holes in many kinds of light.
hint: It is a telescope in space.

q: Why does a turning satellite keep turning after the push stops?
options: Nothing in space slows it down
explain: With no air to rub against, a spin continues until a push the other way stops it: Newton’s first law, for turning.
hint: There is no air to rub against.

q: Which kinds of light can AstroSat see?
explain: AstroSat observes in ultraviolet, visible and X-ray light at the same time.
hint: More than just the colours our eyes see.

q: Which NASA spacecraft did Chandrayaan-2’s orbiter move away from?
explain: In October 2021 ISRO moved the orbiter so it would not pass too close to NASA’s LRO.
hint: Its name says it scouts the Moon.

q: Why did both orbiters come close over the Moon’s pole?
explain: Polar orbits pass over the north and south poles every lap, so paths can cross there.
hint: Their paths both cross the top and bottom of the Moon.

q: A small forward push lifts your orbit the most where?
options: A quarter of an orbit later
explain: A push changes the opposite side of the orbit the most, half an orbit after the burn.
hint: On the far side of the Moon from the burn.

q: What is NavIC?
explain: NavIC (Navigation with Indian Constellation) gives positions over India, like GPS.
hint: India’s own version of GPS.

q: How does a navigation satellite tell you how far away it is?
options: By its size in the sky
By how long its signal takes to arrive
explain: The signal travels at the speed of light, so its travel time gives the distance.
hint: Signals travel at the speed of light.

q: How many distance circles do you need, at least, to find one spot on a map?
explain: Two circles usually cross at two places; a third picks the right one. (In 3D, receivers use at least four satellites.)
hint: Count the circles in the level.

q: Why do rockets drop empty stages?
options: So they stop carrying useless weight
explain: A lighter rocket speeds up more with the same push, so empty tanks and engines are thrown away.
hint: A lighter rocket speeds up more.

q: What fuel does LVM3’s C25 cryogenic stage use?
explain: Cryogenic means super-cold: liquid hydrogen burns with liquid oxygen.
hint: Two super-cold liquids.

q: Why does a rocket lean over as it climbs?
options: To build sideways speed for orbit
explain: Orbit means falling sideways so fast you keep missing the ground: about 7.8 km/s sideways.
hint: Orbit means falling sideways, very fast.

q: Why did Vikram hover at about 150 m before landing?
options: To check the ground for a safe spot
explain: Its hazard-detection cameras checked for boulders and slopes, then it moved to a safer spot.
hint: It looked for boulders and slopes.

q: Once you are sliding sideways in space, what stops you?
options: Only a push the other way
explain: With no air, only a thrust in the opposite direction removes sideways speed (Newton’s first law).
hint: Newton’s first law.

q: About how fast was Vikram falling when its legs touched the Moon?
explain: Vikram touched down at about 0.98 m/s, well inside its legs’ 3 m/s limit.
hint: Slower than walking pace.

q: About how fast does Pragyan drive?
explain: Pragyan moves at about 1 cm/s, carefully, on rough ground.
hint: About a fingertip’s width every second.

q: Why did Pragyan have to finish its work in about 14 days?
explain: A day on the Moon lasts about 14 Earth days; then comes a freezing two-week night with no sunlight for power.
hint: A day on the Moon lasts about two Earth weeks.

q: Which element did Pragyan confirm in the soil near the Moon’s south pole?
explain: Pragyan’s LIBS instrument confirmed sulphur in the lunar soil near the south pole.
hint: A yellow element.

q: What is special about the L1 point?
options: The pulls of the Sun and Earth balance there
It has no gravity at all
explain: At L1 a spacecraft goes round the Sun in step with Earth, because the two pulls (and its motion) balance.
hint: A balancing point between two big pulls.

q: About how far is L1 from Earth?
explain: L1 is about 1.5 million km from Earth, towards the Sun.
hint: About four times as far as the Moon.

q: Why does Aditya-L1 need small engine nudges to stay near L1?
options: L1 is unstable, so small drifts grow
The Sun pushes it away every day
explain: L1 is like a ball on a hilltop: any small drift grows, so small corrections keep it on track.
hint: Like a ball balanced on a hilltop.

q: How long does a geostationary satellite take to go once round Earth?
explain: It goes round once for every spin of Earth, so it seems to hang still over one place.
hint: The same as one spin of Earth.

q: About how high is a geostationary orbit?
explain: Geostationary orbit is 35,786 km above the equator.
hint: Almost a tenth of the way to the Moon.

q: If a satellite speeds up, its orbit gets higher, and it goes round…
explain: Higher orbits take longer, so speeding up actually makes it fall behind and drift west.
hint: Higher orbits take longer.

q: What is Pushpak?
explain: Pushpak is ISRO’s Reusable Launch Vehicle test craft that lands on a runway like an aeroplane.
hint: It lands on a runway like an aeroplane.

q: What lifted Pushpak up for its landing tests?
explain: An Indian Air Force Chinook helicopter carried it up and released it 4.5 km high.
hint: A helicopter with two big rotors.

q: Why does a glider pull up just before touching down?
options: To climb back to the clouds
To slow its sinking for a soft landing
explain: Pulling up (the flare) adds lift for a moment, so it sinks gently onto the runway.
hint: Pilots call it the flare.

q: Who is known as the father of the Indian space programme?
explain: Dr Vikram Sarabhai founded India’s space research; the Vikram lander is named after him.
hint: The Vikram lander carries his name.

q: Where was India’s first rocket launched, in 1963?
explain: A small sounding rocket was launched from Thumba, near Thiruvananthapuram, on 21 November 1963.
hint: Near Thiruvananthapuram.

q: What is the name of India’s human spaceflight programme?
explain: Gaganyaan will carry Indian astronauts into orbit in an Indian spacecraft.
hint: ‘Gagan’ means sky.

q: Which planet spins on its side?
explain: Uranus is tilted about 98°, so it rolls around the Sun on its side.
hint: An ice giant visited only by Voyager 2.

q: Roughly how fast does light travel?
explain: Light travels about 300,000 km every second.
hint: Light could go round Earth more than 7 times in one second.

q: How long does Earth take to go round the Sun?
explain: One trip round the Sun is one year, about 365.25 days.
hint: One year.

q: What do we call a space rock that reaches the ground?
explain: A meteor is the streak of light; a piece that survives to the ground is a meteorite.
hint: If it burns up in the air, it is just a meteor.

q: Which galaxy do we live in?
explain: Our Solar System is in the Milky Way, a spiral galaxy of hundreds of billions of stars.
hint: Its name comes from how it looks in a dark sky.

q: Which star is closest to Earth?
explain: The Sun is a star, about 150 million km away. The next closest is Proxima Centauri.
hint: You see it every day.

q: Which Indian-born woman astronaut flew on the Space Shuttle?
explain: Kalpana Chawla, born in Karnal, Haryana, flew on the Space Shuttle in 1997 and 2003.
hint: She was born in Karnal, Haryana.

q: In 2025, which Indian astronaut flew to the International Space Station?
explain: Group Captain Shubhanshu Shukla flew to the ISS on the Axiom-4 mission in June 2025.
hint: An Indian Air Force pilot chosen for Gaganyaan.
